```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`reintervals` computes four interval types for a linear mixed model, and picks
the computational engine automatically from the fitted model. This vignette is
the map: given your model, which intervals are available, which method you get
by default, and what to watch for.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(reintervals)
library(lme4)
```

## The four intervals

| Verb | Answers |
|---|---|
| `ci_lmm()` | Confidence interval for the **mean**. |
| `pi_lmm()` | Prediction interval for a **single future observation**. |
| `ti_lmm()` | Tolerance interval covering a **proportion `P` of the population**. |
| `new_group_mean_lmm()` | Interval for the **mean of one new, as-yet-unobserved group** (CInew / new-batch-mean). |

## The four engines

| Engine (`method`) | Used for | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| `ems-mls` | Random-intercept designs and the balanced fixed-slope design (expected-mean-square / observed-information MLS); the new-group-mean interval on nested, crossed, and one-way-with-covariates designs. | Francq, Lin & Hoyer (2019) |
| `anova-mls` | Single-observation / unbalanced fixed-slope (stability) tolerance intervals, and — without a covariate — the intercept-only one-way tolerance interval (unweighted group-mean ANOVA); the new-group-mean interval on every fixed-slope design and on the intercept-only one-way design. | Montes, Burdick & Leblond (2019); Hoffman & Kringle (2005) |
| `reml-mls` | Random-slope closed-form intervals. | Graybill–Wang MLS two-component bound (Graybill & Wang 1980); generalized Satterthwaite df |
| `gpq` | Random-slope batch-mean target, and random-slope tolerance intervals when the fit is singular or the closed form's Satterthwaite df is unavailable (generalized pivotal quantity, Monte-Carlo). | Oliva-Aviles & Hauser (2025) |

The engine is chosen automatically from the model's structure; `method =` lets
you pin it (within what is valid — see below).

## Which interval for which model

Read down to your model structure. `ems`, `anova`, `reml`, `gpq` are the engine
tags; superscript letters are explained below. CI_new (`new_group_mean_lmm()`)
targets the true mean of a new innermost cell: a new group (one-way), a new
B-within-A cell (nested), a new (a, b) cell (crossed), or a new lot at `t0`
(fixed and random slope) ^h^.

| Model / situation | CI | PI | TI | CI_new |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Random intercept — one-way, intercept only (`y ~ 1 + (1 | g)`; balanced or unbalanced) | `ems` | `ems` | **`anova`** ^g^ | **`anova`** ^h^ |
| Random intercept — one-way with covariates (balanced or unbalanced) | `ems` | `ems` | `ems` | `ems` ^h^ |
| Random intercept — nested (balanced or unbalanced) | `ems` | `ems` | `ems` | `ems` |
| Random intercept — crossed **with** interaction (balanced/unbalanced; >2 VCs) | `ems` | `ems` | `ems` | `ems` |
| Random intercept — crossed **no** interaction | `ems` | `ems` | **error** ^a^ | **error** ^a^ |
| Random intercept — ≥4 grouping factors (off-catalog) | `ems` | `ems` | **error** ^a^ | **error** ^a^ |
| Random intercept + fixed slope — clean balanced | `ems` | `ems` | `ems` | **`anova`** ^h^ |
| Random intercept + fixed slope — single-obs / staggered / unbalanced | `ems` ^b^ | `ems` ^b^ | **`anova`** ^c^ | **`anova`** ^h^ |
| Random slope — non-singular, future-observation target | `reml` | `reml` | `reml` | `reml` |
| Random slope — non-singular, batch-mean target (`over = "group_mean"`) | — ^d^ | — ^d^ | **`gpq`** | — ^d^ |
| Random slope — singular fit, or TI Satterthwaite df unavailable | `reml` ^e^ | `reml` ^e^ | **`gpq`** ^e^ | `reml` ^e^ |
| Random slope + ≥2 fixed effects | **error** ^f^ | **error** ^f^ | **error** ^f^ | **error** ^f^ |

^a^ These designs have no closed-form variance decomposition, so `ti_lmm()`
and `new_group_mean_lmm()` signal a clear error. CI and PI remain available.

^b^ On fixed-slope data with single-observation lots the EMS confidence and
prediction intervals can be anti-conservative (too narrow); `ci_lmm()` and
`pi_lmm()` emit a warning when at least one lot has a single observation. The
interval is returned unchanged. Staggered designs whose lots all have two or
more observations do not warn.

^c^ `ti_lmm()` re-routes to the Montes ANOVA closed form (`anova-mls`), which is
validated for this structure.

^d^ `over = "group_mean"` (batch-mean) is a `ti_lmm()` argument only, and the
batch-mean *tolerance* target is random-slope-only in this version. For other
designs, `new_group_mean_lmm()` gives an interval for a new batch's mean — it is
available for random-intercept, fixed-slope, and random-slope models. The
coverage verbs carry no batch-mean target.

^e^ For a singular random-slope fit, the tolerance interval switches to the GPQ
engine (the closed form's batch-mean/singular behavior is not validated); CI, PI,
and CI_new stay on the closed form, flagged `singular`. The tolerance interval
also switches to GPQ, at a given `t0`, on a non-singular fit whose Satterthwaite
df for the between-group or residual variance is unavailable (the closed form's
containment fallback fired; such fits sit near the variance-component
boundary). `attr(., "diagnostics")$route_reason` reports `"singular"` or
`"df_unavailable"`.

^f^ Random-slope support is limited to a single continuous covariate (`~ 1 + x`)
in this version — time in the stability use case, but any continuous predictor works.

^g^ `ti_lmm()` uses the Hoffman & Kringle (2005) closed form (`anova-mls`),
the one-way case of the unweighted-means ANOVA interval.
`method = "ems-mls"` gives the Francq et al. (2019) interval instead; the two
coincide on balanced data with a non-singular fit and differ on singular or
unbalanced data.

^h^ The new-group-mean interval is `centre ± t_df · sqrt(W)`. On fixed-slope and
intercept-only one-way designs (`anova-mls`) the centre is the unweighted mean of
the lot means (at `t0` for a fixed slope) and `W = S2_L (1 + 1/I)` plus, with a
slope, `S2_E (t0 - tbar)^2 / S_tt`, with a Satterthwaite df (`I - 1` without a
slope). On nested and one-way-with-covariates designs (`ems-mls`)
`W = V_F + Σ k_j EMS_j` over the random terms with the top factor's df `A - 1`;
on crossed designs the same `W` with a Satterthwaite df in which `V_F` is
attached to the two main effects. `W`, `df`, and the rule are in
`attr(., "diagnostics")`. The one-way-with-covariates construction has not been
validated by simulation.

## Confidence-interval degrees of freedom

For random-intercept models (including the fixed-slope design), `ci_lmm()` uses
a Satterthwaite df built from the observed-information covariance of the
variance components. When that df is unavailable — typically on a singular fit
— it falls back to the SAS-style containment df: `A - 1` for one-way and nested
designs (one less per between-group fixed effect) and `min(A, B) - 1` for
crossed designs. Kenward-Roger df are used only on request,
`control = lmm_interval_control(ci_df = "kenward-roger")`, which needs the
**pbkrtest** package and errors if it is not installed, so results never depend
on which packages happen to be installed. The df source is reported in
`attr(., "diagnostics")$df_method`. Random-slope models use their own
generalized Satterthwaite df.

## One-sided intervals

Every verb accepts `sides = "lower"` or `"upper"`.

| Interval | One-sided construction | Status |
|---|---|---|
| CI, PI, new-group mean (all engines) | same centre, variance, and df as the two-sided interval, with `t_{1-alpha}` | available |
| TI, `anova-mls` (Hoffman-Kringle one-way; Montes fixed slope) | Hoffman's (2010) one-sided limit: `Yhat ∓ (z_P sqrt(U) + z_{1-alpha} sqrt(Vhat(Yhat)))` with the two-sided MLS bound `U` | available (published: Hoffman 2010; Montes et al. 2019) |
| TI, `ems-mls` (Francq) | the same structure with Francq's MLS bound on the total variance and `Vhat = V_F` | provisional, pending validation |
| TI, random slope | GPQ by default (`route_reason = "one_sided"`); a forced `reml-mls` uses Hoffman's structure | GPQ available; `reml-mls` provisional |

## Choosing the method by hand

By default `method = "auto"` selects the one engine valid for your model. For
most models there is no alternative — requesting a different engine errors. Only
three cases offer a genuine choice, all for tolerance intervals:

- **Intercept-only one-way TI** (`y ~ 1 + (1 | g)`, one grouping factor, no
  covariates): default `"anova-mls"` (Hoffman & Kringle 2005, balanced or
  unbalanced, two-sided); `"ems-mls"` (Francq et al. 2019) is also accepted. The
  two coincide on balanced data with a non-singular fit and differ on singular or
  unbalanced data.
- **Fixed-slope (random intercept + fixed slope) TI, any design:** `"anova-mls"`
  (Montes) and `"ems-mls"` are both accepted, clean balanced designs included. The
  default is `"ems-mls"` on a clean balanced design and `"anova-mls"` on a
  single-observation / unbalanced one (validated for that structure); forcing
  `"ems-mls"` there takes the path flagged as anti-conservative, so it's mainly
  for comparison.
- **Random-slope TI (future-observation target):** default `"reml-mls"` (closed
  form) on a non-singular fit; `"gpq"` (Monte-Carlo) is also valid and becomes the
  default automatically when the fit is singular. For the batch-mean target, only
  `"gpq"` is available.

## Worked examples


A random-intercept + fixed-slope model — every verb uses `ems-mls`:

```{r ex-ems}
fm <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
ci_lmm(fm, newdata = data.frame(Days = 5))
ti_lmm(fm, newdata = data.frame(Days = 5), P = 0.99)
```

A random-slope model — the verbs use the `reml-mls` closed form:

```{r ex-slope}
fs <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
ci_lmm(fs, newdata = data.frame(Days = 5))
```

The batch-mean tolerance interval on the same slope model uses GPQ (Monte-Carlo
set a seed for reproducibility):

```{r ex-gpq}
ti_lmm(fs, newdata = data.frame(Days = 5), P = 0.99,
       over = "group_mean",
       control = lmm_interval_control(seed = 1, M = 20000))
```

## Limitations in this version

- **One-sided tolerance limits** on the `ems-mls` engine and on a forced
  `reml-mls` are provisional, pending validation (see "One-sided intervals").
- **Tolerance and new-group-mean intervals** require a closed-form variance
  decomposition; for crossed-no-interaction and ≥4-factor designs, `ti_lmm()` and
  `new_group_mean_lmm()` error (CI and PI remain available).
- **Batch-mean tolerance intervals** (`over = "group_mean"`) are currently
  available only for random-slope models; a random-intercept batch-mean tolerance
  interval is not currently available.
- **Random-slope** models are supported for a single continuous covariate (time
  in the stability design, but any continuous predictor works).

## References

- Francq, B. G., Lin, D., & Hoyer, W. (2019). Confidence, prediction, and
  tolerance in linear mixed models. *Statistics in Medicine*, 38(30), 5603–5622.
  <doi:10.1002/sim.8386>
- Montes, R. O., Burdick, R. K., & Leblond, D. J. (2019). Simple approach to
  calculate random effects model tolerance intervals to set release and
  shelf-life specification limits of pharmaceutical products. *PDA Journal of
  Pharmaceutical Science and Technology*. <doi:10.5731/pdajpst.2018.008839>
- Hoffman, D., & Kringle, R. (2005). Two-sided tolerance intervals for balanced
  and unbalanced random effects models. *Journal of Biopharmaceutical
  Statistics*, 15(2), 283–293. <doi:10.1081/BIP-200048826>
- Hoffman, D., & Kringle, R. (2007). A total error approach for the validation
  of quantitative analytical methods. *Pharmaceutical Research*, 24(6),
  1157–1164. <doi:10.1007/s11095-007-9242-3>
- Hoffman, D. (2010). One-sided tolerance limits for balanced and unbalanced
  random effects models. *Technometrics*, 52(3), 303–312.
  <doi:10.1198/TECH.2010.09171>
- Graybill, F. A., & Wang, C.-M. (1980). Confidence intervals on nonnegative
  linear combinations of variances. *Journal of the American Statistical
  Association*, 75(372), 869–873.
- Oliva-Aviles, C., & Hauser, P. (2025). *Technometrics*, 67(2), 193–202.
  <doi:10.1080/00401706.2024.2407324>
